summary: The article accurately reports on the Bengaluru ITAT ruling regarding capital gains exemption for multiple property sales and provides generally correct information on capital gains taxation and exemptions under Sections 54 and 54F. Some minor details regarding the holding period for long-term capital assets and the specific tax rate for LTCG on property could be more precise based on recent amendments.

claims.claim: A Bengaluru resident successfully claimed full tax exemption on capital gains from selling 17 apartments, amounting to ₹11.8 crore.
claims.note: The Bengaluru ITAT ruled in favor of the taxpayer, Pavan Kumar Agarwal, who sold 17 flats and had capital gains of ₹11.8 crore, allowing the full exemption.

claims.claim: If you sell a property within 24 months (two years) of acquiring it, the gains are considered short-term.
claims.note: For immovable property (land or building), the holding period to be considered short-term is 24 months or less.

claims.claim: LTCG on property is typically taxed at a flat rate of 20% after factoring in indexation benefits.
claims.note: While 20% with indexation was a common rate, recent changes (post-Budget 2024) indicate a default LTCG rate of 12.5% without indexation for property acquired on or after July 23, 2024. Resident individuals and HUFs selling property acquired before this date may still opt for the lower of 12.5% without indexation or 20% with indexation.

claims.claim: For Section 54, if the capital gain does not exceed ₹2 crore, an assessee can opt to invest in two residential houses in India. This option is available only once in the lifetime of the assessee.
claims.note: With effect from Assessment Year 2020-21, a taxpayer has an option to invest in two residential house properties in India to claim Section 54 exemption, provided the long-term capital gain does not exceed ₹2 crores. This option can be exercised only once in a lifetime.

claims.claim: For Section 54F, the proceeds from the sale of a non-residential asset must generally be invested in *one* residential house in India to claim the exemption, unless the aforementioned ₹2 crore limit and lifetime option apply.
claims.note: Section 54F generally requires investment in one residential house. The ₹2 crore limit and lifetime option for two houses specifically apply to Section 54 (sale of a residential house), not Section 54F (sale of any long-term capital asset other than a residential house).

claims.claim: If you have not invested the capital gains into a new house before the due date for filing your income tax return for the year in which the original asset was sold, you must deposit the unutilised capital gains amount into a Capital Gains Account Scheme (CGAS) with a public sector bank.
claims.note: The Capital Gains Account Scheme (CGAS) allows taxpayers to deposit unutilised capital gains in public sector banks before the income tax return filing deadline to claim exemption.

claims.claim: If the amount deposited in CGAS is not utilised for purchasing or constructing the new house within the stipulated timelines (2 or 3 years), the unutilised amount becomes taxable as LTCG in the financial year in which the 2-year or 3-year period expires.
claims.note: If the amount deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme is not utilised within the specified period (generally 2 or 3 years), the unutilised amount will be taxed as income of the previous year in which the specified period expires.

claims.claim: NRIs are eligible to claim exemptions under Section 54 and 54F, provided all the conditions, including the reinvestment in a residential house located in India, are met.
claims.note: NRIs are eligible to claim exemptions under Section 54 and 54F, provided the reinvestment is made in a residential property located in India and other conditions are met.

article_title: Bengaluru Landowner's ₹11.8 Cr Tax Win: Capital Gains Explained
